subject: RFP: Token hedge & surge amortization — commercial scenarios and credit rules

Subject: RFP: Commercial appendix — can you provide amortization examples for surge credits?

Ben,

Thanks for the quick review of the RFP. Procurement wants a clear explanation and a worked example for what you call the 'amortized surge credit' approach — specifically:

- How overages are converted into pre-paid credits that amortize against future invoices,
- The reconciliation cadence and rules (quarterly, true-up thresholds), and
- How refunds vs. credits are handled for terminated pilots.

We have the commercial appendix attached (NC_RFP_Commercial_Appendix_v1.xlsx). Can you provide 1) a short narrative we can include in the RFP response, and 2) a numerical example (6 months) showing invoice adjustments?

Also include any gating language around committed vs. burst traffic and whether credits expire. We need this by end of week to include in our consolidated response.

Regards,

Subject: Re: RFP: Commercial appendix — can you provide amortization examples for surge credits?

Janet,

Thanks — attached is a concise narrative and a worked numeric example (see redwood-pricing-scenarios-v3.pdf). Key points up front:

1) Concept: Surge overages are converted to "Prepaid Surge Credits" which are amortized across the following N billing periods (we typically use N=6 months for pilots/POCs and N=12 months for multi-year committed agreements). Credits reduce per-token invoice charges until depleted.

2) Triggering events: Credits arise when monthly usage exceeds the committed token bucket by more than the agreed burst cushion (default 20%). Only the excess portion is eligible for conversion to credits; usage within the cushion is billed at the overage rate.

3) Amortization & reconciliation rules:
   - Example amortization window: 6 months.
   - Each month, a portion of the surge credit is applied to the next invoice as a line-item "Surge Credit (amortized)".
   - If cumulative usage drops and credits remain, they apply until exhausted or the contract end-date.
   - Quarterly true-up: a reconciliation run compares committed vs. actual tokens and adjusts outstanding credit balances (positive or negative) with the next invoice.

4) Credit expiry & termination:
   - Credits created from overages during an active term remain valid for the amortization window even if the customer terminates early; unamortized credits at termination are retained by the customer and can be applied to any outstanding balance within 90 days.

5) Refunds: We prefer crediting versus cash refunds. Cash refunds are allowed only in negotiated enterprise SOWs and require finance sign-off.

6) Pricing interaction: Credits do not change the underlying per-token pricing tiers; they simply offset billed amounts. For customers on volume-tier discounts, credit application follows the effective rate band for the invoice month.

Numeric example (excerpt):
   - Committed: 500M tokens / month at $0.0008/token (committed unit price)
   - Actual month 1 usage: 700M tokens -> 200M overage
   - Burst cushion: 20% of commit = 100M tokens (billed at overage rate $0.0012/token)
   - Eligible surge to convert to credit = 200M - 100M = 100M tokens -> credit value = 100M * $0.0012 = $120,000
   - Amortize $120,000 over 6 months = $20,000/month credit applied to invoices 2-7
   - If in month 3 usage drops below commit and invoices show no overages, surplus credits continue to offset until exhausted or contract end; quarterly true-up reconciles any under/over application.

I've attached the PDF with a month-by-month table and a second scenario showing a 12-month amortization for committed enterprise customers.

Next steps: If this approach is acceptable, we can add the few lines of contract language the RFP team requested and surface the example table in the response pack. Open to modifying the amortization window or cushion percent if NovaCorp prefers different economics.

Best,

Janet – adding one operational clarification that procurement asked about in a separate call: how we treat negative amortization when refunds would be due (i.e., when previously applied surge credits exceed subsequent invoices because usage drops drastically).

Operational rule we propose:
- Negative balances after a quarterly true-up are carried as a credit on the customer's account and can be used to offset any outstanding or future invoices for 90 days.
- If after 90 days the negative balance remains, the customer may request a cash refund; refunds for amounts > $50k require Finance approval and are processed within 60 days.
- For pilot agreements (<= 6 months), we will process refunds automatically for negative balances > $5k; smaller amounts will be applied as credit.

I'll also note that for enterprise contracts we typically include a fail-safe: automatic fallback to a lower-cost compatible model if latency-sensitive production traffic would otherwise be degraded by aggressive burst-handling rules; this keeps customer SLAs intact while protecting revenue.

Marissa
